Part 2: renal cell carcinoma and its types, Wilms tumor, and urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis. Tags: beyond source = added by me, not in his materials.

1. Clinical Presentation of Renal Tumors

  • Classic triad: flank pain, hematuria (often microscopic, with episodes of gross hematuria) and a palpable flank mass. Only about 10% of patients have the full triad.
  • Nonspecific: fatigue, anemia (blood loss, general tumor effect), weight loss. Fatigue and weight loss go with any neoplasm.
  • About 50% of renal cell carcinomas are found incidentally (CT done for something else, or a lab finding such as hemoglobin of 19).
  • Renal cell carcinoma is "the Great Mimicker" and is also known for odd metastases (he recalls one to the forehead). It is a tumor to consider when a metastasis has an unknown primary.

Paraneoplastic syndromes (mostly renal cell carcinoma)

SyndromeCause
Erythrocytosis (high hemoglobin)Erythropoietin made by the tumor (the kidney normally makes it)
HypercalcemiaParathyroid hormone-related peptide (like squamous cell carcinoma of the lung)
Cushing syndromeACTH production
Feminization or masculinizationHormone production
Hepatic dysfunctionParaneoplastic
CachexiaSystemic effect
HypertensionRenin production beyond source
Point to ponderA neoplasm with elevated hemoglobin: think renal cell carcinoma (erythropoietin), hepatocellular carcinoma, and cerebellar hemangioblastoma. The patient may present with a high hemoglobin found incidentally, or with symptoms of polycythemia.

2. Important Benign Renal Tumors

Angiomyolipoma

  • Composition: fat (lipoma), smooth muscle (myo), thick-walled blood vessels (angio).
  • Associated with tuberous sclerosis (TSC1 and TSC2 proteins), but most occur sporadically in people without it.
  • Benign: does not metastasize, though it can still grow and cause complications. Grossly tan-yellow with red areas (slide question).
  • Desmin positive in the muscle component. Smooth muscle may not be obvious in every section.
Slide: angiomyolipoma. Blood vessels (white arrows), smooth muscle around them (left), and adipose tissue. The right section has little good smooth muscle.
Slide question10 cm tan-yellow renal tumor with red areas; mature fat, thick-walled vessels, desmin-positive cells; hereditary syndrome? → tuberous sclerosis (D).

Papillary renal adenoma

  • Small: <1 (up to 3) cm. Size to separate adenoma from carcinoma is controversial. If <5 mm with papillary growth, it can be considered benign.
  • Common with increasing age, often multiple.
  • Papillary architecture (he thinks of a cross-section of a sea anemone).
  • Mimic: a tiny yellow nodule on the kidney surface may be ectopic adrenal tissue.
Slide: multiple renal adenomas (arrows) on the surface; papillary architecture on microscopy.

Medullary fibroma (renomedullary interstitial cell tumor)

  • Fibrous tissue in the renal medulla. Common at autopsy in adults; probably the most common benign kidney tumor he sees.
  • Well-defined nodules of a few millimeters, near the corticomedullary junction; low cellularity with scattered nuclei in fibrous tissue.
Slide: medullary fibroma (arrow), a small well-defined nodule; microscopy shows sparse spindle cells in fibrous tissue.

Mesoblastic nephroma

  • Hamartoma of spindled or fibroblastic cells. Occurs in children, first 3 months of life.
  • Differentiate from nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor): Wilms usually has three components, one of them spindled, but can be monophasic (all mesenchymal), which looks like mesoblastic nephroma. Mesoblastic nephroma is benign; Wilms is malignant.
  • Ill-defined margins and can recur (hard to excise completely); tumor cells infiltrate among normal glomeruli.
Slide: mesoblastic nephroma. Cut surface of a kidney with a well-circumscribed-appearing pale nodule; spindled cell proliferation.
Slide: mesoblastic nephroma, low and high power; the tumor infiltrates around normal glomeruli, explaining the risk of recurrence.

Oncocytoma

FeatureDetails
Frequency3–7% of renal tumors (Robbins 10%; Rubin 5–10%)
Cell of originIntercalated cells of the collecting ducts (tested on USMLE)
GeneticsLoss of chromosomes 1, 14 and Y
GrossTan with a central scar
MicroscopicLarge cells with finely granular eosinophilic cytoplasm (mitochondria); oncocytic change like Hurthle cells in the thyroid
DifferentialChromophobe renal cell carcinoma (benign vs malignant): Hale’s colloidal iron is positive in chromophobe; DOG1 stain mentioned (not for memorization)
Slide: oncocytoma. Tan nodule with a central scar (arrow); sheets of large eosinophilic granular cells.
Point to ponder: central scarAnother tumor with a central scar is focal nodular hyperplasia of the liver.

Juxtaglomerular cell tumor

  • Benign, also called reninoma: it secretes renin, causing hypertension (often resistant to treatment) that is cured when the tumor is removed.

3. Renal Cell Carcinoma: Overview

DemographicsRisk factors
3% of adult malignancies (12th most common cancer worldwide)
80–85% of malignant kidney tumors
338,000 cases and 100,000 deaths (2012, worldwide)
6th–7th decades, M > F
Incidence increasing; most common in developed countries		Cigarette smoking
Obesity and lack of exercise (BMI >30; 20–25% higher risk per 5-unit BMI rise)
Environmental agents (cadmium)
Hypertension
Acquired polycystic kidney disease (cysts in long-term dialysis patients; not autosomal dominant PKD)

Forms and cell of origin

TypeCell of originFrequency
Clear cellProximal convoluted tubule65–75%
PapillaryDistal convoluted tubule10–15%
ChromophobeIntercalated cells of collecting ducts~5%
Collecting duct carcinoma (and medullary carcinoma)Collecting ducts of Bellini<1%

Rubin counts collecting duct and medullary carcinoma as forms of renal cell carcinoma; Srigley et al. 2013 treat them as separate entities.

Complications

  • Invasion of the renal vein (growth into the vein, up the inferior vena cava, even to the heart). This is not metastasis; hepatocellular carcinoma does it too.
  • Polycythemia (erythropoietin).
  • Other hormones: hypercalcemia, hypertension, Cushing syndrome, feminization or masculinization.
  • Often the primary is unknown and the diagnosis is made from metastases (most commonly lungs and bones).

Staging and management

T stageDefinition
T1<7 cm, limited to kidney
T2>7 cm, limited to kidney
T3Extends into veins or perinephric tissue
T4Beyond Gerota’s fascia and/or into the adrenal gland
  • Management: partial or complete nephrectomy. Possible targeted therapy against mTOR (regulates VEGF).
  • He says to know that 7 cm is the renal cell cutoff (breast cancer: 2 cm).
Slide questions(1) 4.5 cm focally cystic yellow mass with red areas → most likely reason it was found: incidental CT discovery (C), since about half are incidental. (2) 56-year-old with hematuria, 5.5 cm cystic mass, clear cells → 1–2 pack per day smoking history (E); cadmium would need more information, and most people smoke rather than work in a chemical plant.

4. Renal Cell Carcinoma: Subtypes in Detail

Clear cell carcinoma (65–75%)

  • Gross: a yellow (glycogen/lipid) and red (hemorrhage) mass. This is one of the few tumors with a gross appearance characteristic enough to be tested.
  • Microscopic: clear cells (glycogen) lining a delicate fibrovascular network that easily hemorrhages.
  • Cells can look bland yet the tumor is aggressive. Graded by nuclear features (low grade: uniform nuclei, no mitoses; high grade: pleomorphism, mitoses).
  • Can be very cystic: if a "cyst" has a solid, papillary or thickened wall, it is not a simple cyst and needs evaluation.
Slide: clear cell renal cell carcinoma, gross with arrow at the tumor.
Slide: clear cell carcinoma, gross. Yellow glycogen-rich tumor with hemorrhage and necrosis.
Slide: clear cell carcinoma, microscopic. Clear cells and a delicate vascular network (arrows).
Slide: a cystic clear cell carcinoma with abundant hemorrhage and yellow tissue.

Genetics of clear cell carcinoma

  • Mostly sporadic, but also in von Hippel-Lindau disease. Both involve the VHL gene on 3p25.
  • The VHL protein normally degrades hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs); HIFs are transcription factors that stimulate VEGF. Loss of VHL → more VEGF → blood vessel growth, which matches the vascular pathology.

Papillary renal cell carcinoma (10–15%)

  • Gross: yellow (less bright), frequently bilateral and multifocal.
  • Microscopic: papillae with fibrovascular cores, often with foamy macrophages; cells basophilic or acidophilic.
  • Genetics: MET proto-oncogene (7q31), a tyrosine kinase receptor for hepatocyte growth factor (hereditary and some sporadic forms).
Slide: papillary renal cell carcinoma. Papillae with fibrovascular cores (yellow arrows).

Chromophobe renal cell carcinoma (~5%)

  • From intercalated cells of collecting ducts (same origin as oncocytoma).
  • Gross: tan-brown (like oncocytoma). Microscopic: distinct cell membranes, perinuclear halos, Hale's colloidal iron positive.
  • Genetics: multiple whole-chromosome losses (1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17, 21), hypodiploidy.
  • More favorable prognosis than clear cell.
  • Hard to separate from oncocytoma on H&E; do not expect that distinction without extra information.
Slide: oncocytoma (inset) vs chromophobe renal cell carcinoma. They can look very similar.

Collecting duct carcinoma (<1%)

  • Arises from collecting ducts in the medulla. Tubular and papillary structures lined by a single layer of cuboidal cells with a hobnail appearance.
  • Very aggressive; most present with metastases. Deletions 1p, 8p, 9p.
  • Medullary carcinoma (variant): only in people with sickle cell trait or sickle cell disease.
TumorQuick differentiators
Clear cellYellow-red gross; VHL (3p25); proximal tubule; most common
PapillaryPapillae, foamy macrophages; MET (7q31); bilateral, multifocal
ChromophobeHalos; Hale’s iron positive; multiple chromosome losses; good prognosis
Oncocytoma (benign)Central scar; granular eosinophilic; loss of 1, 14, Y
Collecting duct / medullaryHobnail; aggressive; medullary = sickle cell trait

5. Wilms Tumor (Nephroblastoma)

  • Demographics: third most common organ tumor in children 10 or younger (85% of pediatric renal neoplasms); 1 in 10,000; 98% before 10 years, most at 2–5 years.
  • Gross: tan to gray, soft, homogeneous; may have necrosis, hemorrhage, cystic degeneration (nonspecific).
  • Microscopic: triphasic: blastemal (sheets of small round blue cells), stromal (fibrocytic, myxoid, or skeletal muscle), and epithelial (abortive tubules or glomeruli). Can be monophasic (e.g., all stromal, mimicking mesoblastic nephroma).
  • Precursor: nephrogenic rests (undeveloped glomerulus-like clusters under the capsule).
Slide: Wilms tumor, triphasic: epithelial, blastemal and stromal components.
Slide: nephrogenic rest (arrow), a cluster of immature blue cells beside normal glomeruli.

Prognosis

FeaturePrognosis
Anaplasia (atypical mitoses, large nuclei, hyperchromasia; ~5% of tumors)Unfavorable
No anaplasia (recognized by Beckwith and Palmer)Favorable; different treatment regimen
TP53 mutationWorse; almost always with anaplasia (75% of anaplastic tumors)
Increasing age; LOH of 1p and 16q; tumor volumeWorse

Clinical presentation

  • Abdominal mass, abdominal pain, intestinal obstruction (mass effect), hypertension, hematuria, rupture (friable tumor).

Genetics

  • WT1: tumor suppressor gene regulating transcription of IGF, E-cadherin, PDGF; loss leads to β-catenin degradation problems and altered WNT signaling. Mutated in 10–20% of sporadic tumors.
  • Sporadic Wilms tumor ~90%: WT1 mutation (10–20%), gain of function of β-catenin (CTNNB1), TP53 (poor prognosis), and microRNA processing genes (DROSHA, DGCR8) with fewer mature microRNAs (miR-200 family), which normally assist the mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition. The tumor looks stuck between mesenchyme and epithelium (blastema, stroma).
SyndromeFeaturesGene
WAGRWilms (~30%), aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, retardation (mental)Deletion of WT1 on 11p13 (with PAX6)
Denys-DrashWilms (~90%), gonadal dysgenesis, glomerular mesangial sclerosis → early renal failureDominant negative inactivating WT1 mutation
Beckwith-WiedemannWilms, overgrowth (gigantism to hemihypertrophy), visceromegaly, macroglossia, enlarged adrenal cortical cells; also hepatoblastoma, adrenocortical and pancreatic tumorsWT2 on 11p15.5; genomic imprinting; candidate IGF2 (paternal allele expressed, maternal imprinted; in these Wilms tumors the maternal allele is expressed)
Rule of thumbIf a malignant tumor is bilateral and primary, consider a familial syndrome (not always true, but a good prompt).

6. Urothelial Carcinoma of the Renal Pelvis

  • Terminology: older name transitional cell carcinoma.
  • 5–10% of primary kidney tumors: urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis or calyceal system.
  • Less than 5% of urothelial carcinomas occur above the bladder (most are bladder).
  • Risk factor: cigarette smoking. Field effect: the whole urothelium is exposed to the same carcinogens, so a tumor in the pelvis raises the chance of one in the bladder later.
  • Most are papillary (grow outward) and are graded by nuclear features.
Slide: low-grade papillary transitional cell carcinoma (bland, oriented cells) vs high-grade (pleomorphic, disorganized cells).
Point to ponder: another tumor with a field effectThe upper and lower respiratory tract (laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma and lung cancer in smokers).
LinkSee the lower urinary tract guide for bladder urothelial carcinoma grading, carcinoma in situ and genetics.
